draft.title: Reactions of alkenes
card: An alkene has a C=C double bond. In an addition reaction, the double bond breaks and each carbon bonds to a new atom or group. Only one product forms.

Alkenes add hydrogen (H2) to form an alkane, a halogen such as Br2 to form a dihaloalkane, a hydrogen halide such as HBr to form a haloalkane, and water (H2O) to form an alcohol. Hydrogen needs a metal catalyst such as nickel or platinum. Water addition needs an acid catalyst and is called hydration.
Example: ethene + Br2 gives 1,2-dibromoethane. Ethene + H2O gives ethanol. Each carbon of the double bond gains one new bond.

Bromine water is orange-brown. Shaken with an alkene, it turns colourless as the bromine adds across the double bond. A saturated alkane does not decolourise it quickly in the dark, so this is a test for C=C bonds.
draft.remember: Alkenes react by addition across C=C, and they decolourise bromine water.

a.q: Ethene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst. What is the product?
opts: Ethane
Ethanol
Bromoethane
Ethyne
a.why: Hydrogen adds across the C=C bond, so the alkene becomes an alkane, ethane. Ethanol is the tempting wrong answer, because it forms when water adds, not hydrogen.
a.clue: Which molecule adds to the double bond, and what is left?

b.q: A chemist shakes bromine water with two colourless liquids in the dark. Liquid X stays orange-brown. Liquid Y turns colourless. What does this show?
opts: Y has a C=C bond and X does not
X has a C=C bond and Y does not
Both X and Y contain C=C bonds
Neither X nor Y contains a C=C bond
b.why: Bromine water is decolourised when bromine adds across a C=C bond. Y changed colour, so it has a double bond, while X did not react. X is not the answer because staying orange-brown means no addition took place.
b.clue: Which liquid caused the colour to disappear?

b.best: Y has a C=C bond and X does not

problems.detail: "Only one product forms" is false in general. Unsymmetrical alkenes such as propene give two isomeric products with HBr or H2O (1-bromopropane and 2-bromopropane). Bromine water itself mainly gives a bromoalcohol rather than only the dibromide. The card means no by-product forms, and it should say that instead.
"Only one product forms" uses an absolute claim that overstates the idea and will mislead students meeting unsymmetrical alkenes.

check.summary: Both questions are correct. The card's claim that "only one product forms" in addition is false for unsymmetrical alkenes such as propene with HBr or water. It should say that addition gives no by-product instead.
